report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is not supported by high-quality evidence. Induced abortion does **not** appear to increase a woman’s subsequent risk of breast cancer.

A major collaborative reanalysis of individual-level data from 53 studies (including about 83,000 women with breast cancer in 16 countries) found no increase in risk in studies that collected abortion histories prospectively; it reported a relative risk of 0.93 for induced abortion. The authors concluded that apparent elevations in some retrospective studies were likely due to *reporting/recall bias*—for example, women with breast cancer may be more likely to disclose a prior abortion than comparable women without cancer.

The National Cancer Institute’s expert workshop, which reviewed population, clinical, and animal evidence, likewise concluded that induced abortion (and miscarriage) does not raise subsequent breast-cancer risk. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists reaches the same conclusion and notes the methodological problems in early case-control studies that suggested an association.

This does not mean pregnancy history is irrelevant to breast-cancer risk: age at first full-term birth and other reproductive, genetic, hormonal, and lifestyle factors can matter. But an abortion itself is not established as a breast-cancer risk factor.

Sources:  
- https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(04)15835-2/fulltext  
- https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/abortion-miscarriage-risk  
- https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2009/06/induced-abortion-and-breast-cancer-risk
